title: Prioritized Scheduling
explain: Prioritized scheduling serves the most important waiting work first, usually from a heap keyed by priority and enqueue sequence. Strict priority gives the best latency to the top class but brings starvation, priority inversion, priority inflation and non-preemption. I name the remedies for each, and keep few levels with priority derived from server-side facts.
model:
Structure: a **priority queue** (heap) keyed by `(priority, enqueue_sequence)`. A binary heap is not stable, so without the sequence two equal-priority tasks can come out in any order.

Four failure modes of strict priority, each with a fix:

| Problem | What happens | Remedy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Starvation** | High always arrives, low never runs | **Aging** (`effective = base + rate x wait`), reserved capacity for low classes, or weighted shares ([weighted scheduling](#/sd/f/weighted-scheduling)) |
| **Priority inversion** | Low holds a lock High needs; Medium keeps preempting Low | **Priority inheritance**, or do not share locks across classes |
| **Priority inflation** | Clients label everything urgent | Derive priority from authenticated tier, endpoint or quota; cap each class |
| **No preemption** | Long low job delays urgent work by its remaining runtime | Preempt with checkpointing, or chunk long work |

Keep 3 to 5 levels, document their meaning, and measure queue age **per class**.

The same ranking decides what to drop first in [load shedding](#/sd/f/load-shedding); a [dispatcher](#/sd/f/dispatcher) combines it with fairness; the structure sits in a [wait queue](#/sd/f/wait-queue).

details.q: Interactive jobs keep the pool 100 percent busy for hours under strict priority. What happens to report jobs?
details.a: They starve: they wait as long as any higher-priority job is waiting, possibly indefinitely. Add aging, a reserved slice of capacity, or weighted shares.

details.q: With effective = base + 0.5 x seconds waited, a low task has base 1 and fresh high tasks have base 10. When does the low task tie?
details.a: After 18 s: 1 + 0.5t = 10 gives t = 18. So aging gives a bounded wait. Tune the rate to the longest wait you tolerate.

details.q: Task L holds a mutex, H blocks on it, and medium tasks keep preempting L. What is this and how is it fixed?
details.a: Priority inversion: H is effectively waiting behind M. Priority inheritance lets L run at H's priority until it releases the lock. The Mars Pathfinder bug was this.

details.q: Two tasks of the same priority go into a binary heap keyed only by priority. Which pops first?
details.a: Either: a binary heap does not keep insertion order among equal keys. Use `(priority, sequence)` as the key to make ties FIFO.

details.q: Almost every request on the public API ends up marked `high`. What is the design response?
details.a: Derive priority server-side from authenticated tier, endpoint or quota, and cap each class, rather than trusting a client label. Adding a `critical` level just restarts the inflation.

details.q: Why does preemption matter, and what does it cost?
details.a: Without it, a long low-priority job delays a new urgent one by its whole remaining runtime. Preempting needs the job to be pausable or checkpointed and wastes the work done since the last checkpoint.

prompts.q: Strict priority is simple. Name its failure modes and a remedy for each.
points: Starvation: aging, reserved capacity, weighted shares
Priority inflation: derive priority server-side, cap classes
Non-preemption: preemption with checkpoints or chunking

prompts.q: Design the priority queue for a shared worker pool serving interactive and batch jobs.
points: Heap keyed by priority and sequence
Aging or reserved capacity so batch progresses
Priority from authenticated class, not client header

prompts.q: Explain priority inversion with an example and its fix.
points: Low holds a lock High needs
Medium preempts Low so High waits behind Medium
Or avoid sharing locks across classes
